Simulacra is an interesting horror game where the events unfold through a phone screen.

Story:

You play as an unnamed man/woman. We find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna, we find a message of her begging for help and well we launch into an investigation to figure out how to save her.

The story in Simulacra is quite intriguing and all the research you do to figure out what happened to Anna and all the people around her, is quite interesting, because you go through many sites, reading articles and text messages, most of it having some decent writing behind it.

Graphics:

Well the only graphics in this is your phone. The phone has it's own OS named Iris and it's styled after an android phone. It looks quite convincing. You definitely know what each app represents so the art team definitely nailed the look of a smart phone.

Audio:

The acting is pretty sub-par, the actress that plays Anna is the only one that is semi-decent, but everyone else does a pretty mediocre job. However where the game shines the most is in it's audio design. The noises you hear around you when you browse the phone send a shiver down your spine. It could be something simple, like a small whisper to a creepy silent laugh. 

Gameplay:

Simulacra is mostly a puzzle solving game, where you have goals and you have to figure out how solve and these puzzles have a pretty decent design. A liked quite a few of the puzzles and how fresh they felt.

These puzzles range from pretty simple to sometimes head scratching. But it never felt cryptic and actually quite a few of the puzzles required a really logical solution and it felt like it would be something I would do in real life. 

You can do a bunch of research by reading articles, reading text messages so there's a lot of stuff to do in the phone. Also not to mention there's multiple choices throughout the story and multiple endings for you to achieve. 

Verdict:

Simulacra is a pretty unique horror game and it's story is pretty intriguing. With multiple endings and a really interesting plot I loved my time with this game and honestly I suggest giving it a shot at full price.

Pros:
+ Story is pretty intriguing
+ Nails the look of a smartphone perfectly
+ Multiple choices lead to different outcomes and endings
+ Great puzzles

Cons:
- Acting is not good whatsoever 

Final Rating:
8.5/10

It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

Pretty good, truth to be told.

After receiving a mysterious phone, you quickly realize it belongs to a missing young girl, and so you start investigating over her disappearance. Using real life-like apps mimicking twitter, facebook, and Gmail (among others), you'll collect proofs, find connections and chat with the girl's acquaintances to discover an ominous truth.

The ending is a bit of a letdown, but the experience as a whole is engaging.

The game's realization did allow for some immersion and suspension of disbelief and, while there are times where as a player you are pushed in a direction you would not choose, the game flows otherwise quite nicely.

While you are investigating there are some things to do on the side: ominous messages to translate, numbers to use to unlock secret messages, etc. I don't know how many of them are around, but the one I found were a nice diversion.

Acting and voice-acting are also enjoyable most of the time: you have the impression to deal with real people and not actors, usually.

There is not much as far as audio effects are concerned, with the exception of some creepy sound ambiances in superb 3D that did actually made me jump a couple of times.

Also, the game is supposed to be replayable, there are different endings but, frankly after you find out what was all about, I don't see why one should actually do it, unless really really into the game.

All in one a pretty good game, especially for the price.

This game is terrifying and interesting all at the same time. A really neat concept where your choices matter. Easily recommend.

The Good Stuff:

The layout and idea behind the game is pretty cool. I like how each "app" generally feels like a real app where you can do whatever, like comment of peoples posts or call random numbers. It is really neat design idea and it is well executed.

I also enjoyed a few of the more difficult puzzles, as they really added a sense of immersion into digging through someone's phone. The puzzles are mainly pretty easy, but the game doesn't baby you through them at all, so you feel smart when you manage to pull of something a bit more complicated.

The Bad Stuff:

For me, story is one of the most important parts of a game like this, and unfortunately SIMULACRA fails to deliver a good one.

Mild Spoilers: [spoiler]While the ending tried to be Black Mirror-esque, I feel like the story fails to properly set up the ending, so it kinda comes out of nowhere. Also, many things in the story aren't well explained or left to Deus Ex Machina[/spoiler]

There are multiple endings, and you will get an idea of what they all are when you finish the game. Some of the potential outcomes have me slightly curious, but not enough to replay it to see them. Perhaps the story would have been more interesting had I gotten a different ending.

I am not a huge fan of horror, but I have played games like Prey and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that have a creepy horror feel. The creepiness of SIMULACRA lasts only about the first 30 mins and then you become generally innoculated.

The main title song was also pretty cheesy.

As many other reviews have pointed out, some of the voice acting is on the level of "so bad it's hilarious".

I understand that with a smaller scale game like this it is difficult, but I felt like the chat options often strong-armed me into things I didn't want to say, which made things like [spoiler]gaining Taylor's trust[/spoiler] feel unfair.

The Bottom Line: If you want a game with a good story, there are better games. If you want a game where choices matter, there are better games. If you want a horror game, there are better games. If you just want to see a cool mechanic in action, then you might want to check it out.

So, I'd say overall, I really did like this game.  The jumpscares are by far the worst part of it, as it's honestly the cheapest form of horror, but the atmosphere was built beautifully.  The actors did a great job making their acting believable.  Greg's actor started off sounding very off, but started getting more and more believable as the game went on.
As for the plot, it's very clearly inspired by stuff like Metal Gear Solid 2.  Though, admittedly it kinda blew the secret open from the very start, with the very first action by the player being to watch a video that kinda gives the twist away, unsubtly at that.  It was very obvious from the moment they started accusing each other that Greg and Taylor were red herrings, so it felt a little forced that I had to investigate both, even if I was given the opportunity to just believe them.
And, that leads me to the endings.  I got the "Abandon All Hope" ending, and haven't experienced the others, nor do I know what happens in them.  Honestly, I like the idea that no one will trust you if you don't trust them, but I'm not a huge fan of the game constantly hammering at me at the very ending that I fucked up.  Though, I do like the touch that the game conditions you early on to investigate everything, thus requiring some thought from the player to not keep doing that for everyone.
One last thing: I see your Telltale inspiration in telling you the major decision points and comparing it to everyone else's.  And, while it's a good way to keep track of what decisions were hard or easy to make, it kinda pulls the curtain away from how shallow the choice system is, basically telling the player all the choices that actually matter, and showing off just how binary they are.  Not saying you need to put hours of depth into literally hundreds of decisions, just saying showing the player a quantifiable chart of choices gives away the whole thing.

Overall, I'd say this game is definitely worth the $5 my boyfriend paid for it, and I can't wait to see more from this developer

This is a decent "choices matter" voyeuristic psychological thriller with the occasional horror elements (jump scares) that is a must play for horror fans and might be worth checking out on sale for people who like story rich games.  Here is what you need to know:
+Doing all interactions through the phone is very well done.
+Phone UI includes a menu of sorts that shows options of things to do next, and choices you have made.
+All character personalities and writing is well done, but...
-Some of the in-person acting via video seems weak, but part of it could be the inherent awkwardness of characters or their situations.
-The story doesn't seem to really branch out, as it seems more on rails than branching given that choices influence actions that contribute to the end result but don't have a notable impact on the story other than how characters react/feel about you.
-Your in-game surroundings/background and the rare background noises outside of the phone have no relevance to what is actually going on, other than to set a "mood" and randomly have the chance at jump scaring you.  IMO all jump scares should happen within the context of what is ACTUALLY happening, otherwise the other jump scares have faster diminishing returns.

I completed one play through in just under 4 hours and can say that it was fun and engaging the entire time! I'm intrigued by the other endings and interested to see how the experience differs when different choices are made. Well worth the price tag (and I think I even grabbed it on sale).

If you want to enhance the creepiness, I would recommend playing alone in the dark with a headphones, but it's honestly enjoyable to play with others as well, making choices together. Not a full-fledged horror game so if you're weary of scary games, this should be just enough to set you on edge.

I really enjoy this new emergent techno horror/suspense genre that's sprung up over the last few years. It's short, fairly interesting, and well worth the sale price I paid for it. I'd say it's even worth the $5 it normally runs for. It kept me engaged enough to pursue all the endings and it took around eight hours to get them. Recommended if you enjoy this type of game.
